packageRules.description: rules_go and gazelle are version-coupled and were verified together against the pinned Bazel LTS (see docs/design/protean.md section 10). Bumping one without the other is how that verification silently stops holding, so they land as one reviewable PR.

Badger is the store behind protean and signpost, and pkg/kv/badgerkv depends on behaviour its API does not document - notably that Entry.WithTTL truncates expiry to whole seconds. pkg/kv/kvtest is what catches a change there, so a bump needs that suite looked at rather than just a green tick.

The container rules work together and were verified as a set against the pinned Bazel LTS. Bumping one without the others is how that verification silently stops holding, so they land as one reviewable PR.

The base image is pinned by digest in MODULE.bazel, which is what makes the image build reproducible - a tag is a moving reference. Renovate keeps the digest current; the image carries the CA bundle all three services need for outbound TLS, so a bump is worth a sanity check that it still does.
Major Go module bumps (an import-path-changing rename, or a breaking API redesign) need a manual look before merge, not just a passing build.
One pull request for both pins. A release that compiled with one Go version and declared another in go.mod is a release whose stamp lies about how it was built.

customManagers.description: The Go SDK is pinned twice - go_sdk.download in MODULE.bazel, which is the toolchain the Bazel build compiles with, and the go directive in go.mod, which is what actions/setup-go reads. Only the second is a manager Renovate knows, so without this the Bazel pin would sit still while go.mod moved. They have to move together: scripts/bazel-create-status.sh stamps the version it reads from MODULE.bazel, and a govulncheck run against a toolchain one patch behind fails CI on standard-library advisories that a bump already fixed - which is how this manager came to exist.
